claim: Condensin DC is recruited to and spreads from a small number of recruitment elements on the X-chromosome (rex).
source: Condensin DC is recruited to and spreads from a small number of recruitment elements on the X-chromosome (rex) and is required for the formation of topologically associating domains (TADs).
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract and supported by citations to previous work throughout the manuscript.

claim: Condensin DC is required for the formation of topologically associating domains (TADs).
source: Condensin DC is recruited to and spreads from a small number of recruitment elements on the X-chromosome (rex) and is required for the formation of topologically associating domains (TADs).
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by Hi-C data showing TADs on X-chromosome.

claim: When an autosome and X-chromosome are physically fused, spreading of condensin DC into the autosome does not create a TAD.
source: When an autosome and X-chromosome are physically fused, despite the spreading of condensin DC into the autosome, no TAD was created.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by Hi-C data in Figure 2.

claim: Insertion of a strong rex on the X-chromosome results in TAD boundary formation regardless of sequence orientation.
source: Insertion of a strong rex on the X-chromosome results in the TAD boundary formation regardless of sequence orientation.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated by Hi-C data in Figure 3.

claim: When a single strong rex is inserted on an autosome, there is condensin DC recruitment but no spreading or features of a TAD.
source: When the same rex is inserted on an autosome, despite condensin DC recruitment, there was no spreading or features of a TAD.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by ChIP-seq and Hi-C data in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: Insertion of a 'super rex' composed of six rex sites on an autosome leads to recruitment and spreading of condensin DC and formation of TADs.
source: On the other hand, when a 'super rex' composed of six rex sites or three separate rex sites are inserted on an autosome, recruitment and spreading of condensin DC led to the formation of TADs.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated by ChIP-seq and Hi-C data in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: Insertion of three separate rex sites on an autosome leads to recruitment and spreading of condensin DC and formation of loop-anchored TADs.
source: On the other hand, when a 'super rex' composed of six rex sites or three separate rex sites are inserted on an autosome, recruitment and spreading of condensin DC led to the formation of TADs.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated by ChIP-seq and Hi-C data in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: Rex sites are both loading sites and bidirectional barriers for condensin DC.
source: Therefore, recruitment to and spreading from rex sites are necessary and sufficient for recapitulating loop-anchored TADs observed on the X-chromosome. Together our data suggest a model in which rex sites are both loading sites and bidirectional barriers for condensin DC, a one-sided loop-extruder with movable inactive anchor.
evidence: This is the main conclusion stated in the abstract and supported by multiple experiments throughout the manuscript.

claim: Condensin DC is a one-sided loop-extruder with movable inactive anchor.
source: Together our data suggest a model in which rex sites are both loading sites and bidirectional barriers for condensin DC, a one-sided loop-extruder with movable inactive anchor.
evidence: This is the main model proposed based on Hi-C data showing flames rather than perpendicular diagonals.

claim: C. elegans possess condensin IDC (condensin dosage compensation [DC]) that differs from condensins I by a single subunit, the SMC-4 variant DPY-27.
source: In addition to the canonical condensins I and II, C. elegans possess condensin IDC (hereafter condensin dosage compensation [DC]) that differs from condensins I by a single subunit, the SMC-4 variant DPY-27 (Csankovszki et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation to previous work.

claim: Condensin DC binds to both X-chromosomes in hermaphrodites to repress their transcription by a factor of two.
source: Condensin DC binds to both X-chromosomes in hermaphrodites to repress their transcription by a factor of two, equalizing overall X chromosomal transcripts between XX hermaphrodites and XO males (Kruesi et al., 2013; Kramer et al., 2016; Kramer et al., 2015; Albritton and Ercan, 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to previous work.

claim: Condensin DC recruitment to the X-chromosomes is mediated by ~60 recruitment elements on the X-chromosome (rex sites).
source: Condensin DC recruitment to the X-chromosomes is mediated by ~60 recruitment elements on the X-chromosome (rex sites) (Jans et al., 2009; Ercan et al., 2007; Albritton et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to previous work.

claim: Eight strong rex sites function as TAD boundaries and form long-range rex-rex loops on the X-chromosomes.
source: Hi-C analysis in C. elegans embryos indicated that eight strong rex sites function as TAD boundaries and form long-range rex-rex loops on the X-chromosomes (Rowley et al., 2020; Crane et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to previous work.

claim: Recruitment of condensin DC leads to spreading to the entire chromosome, accumulating at hundreds of enhancers, promoters, and other accessible gene regulatory elements.
source: Recruitment of condensin DC leads to spreading to the entire chromosome, accumulating at hundreds of enhancers, promoters, and other accessible gene regulatory elements (Street et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation to previous work.

claim: The X-chromosome harbors TADs separated by rex sites.
source: On the other hand, X-chromosome is globally bound by condensin DC and organized into distinct TADs separated by rex sites, which are strongly bound by the DCC subunits, including SDC-2 and SDC-3 (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 1B Hi-C data.

claim: The loss of SDC-2 results in the failure of condensin DC to localize to the X-chromosome and dissolution of TADs.
source: Unlike the CTCF removal experiments where cohesin remains bound, the loss of SDC-2 results in the failure of condensin DC to localize to the X-chromosome and dissolution of TADs, suggesting that SDC-2 function as both LEF loader and barrier (Crane et al., 2015; Anderson et al., 2019; Pferdehirt et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the results with citations to previous work.

claim: The X-chromosome shows a characteristic enrichment of 3D DNA contacts compared to autosomes.
source: Second, X-chromosome show a characteristic enrichment of 3D DNA contacts compared to autosomes.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by P(s) analysis in Figure 1D.

claim: The mean loop size for C. elegans X-chromosomes is 200 kb in embryo and 125 kb in L3s.
source: Using the same metric, we find that the mean loop size for C. elegans X-chromosomes is 200 kb in embryo and 125 kb in L3s and 400 kb for autosomes.
evidence: This is stated in the results based on analysis of P(s) log-derivative shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The mean loop size for C. elegans autosomes is 400 kb.
source: Using the same metric, we find that the mean loop size for C. elegans X-chromosomes is 200 kb in embryo and 125 kb in L3s and 400 kb for autosomes.
evidence: This is stated in the results based on analysis of P(s) log-derivative shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The X-chromosome shows weaker A/B sub-compartmentalization than autosomes.
source: Third, the X-chromosome shows weaker A/B sub-compartmentalization than autosomes.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by compartment analysis in Figures 1E, 1F, and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: There are no noticeable TADs on chromosome-V side of the X;V fusion.
source: First, there are no noticeable TADs on chromosome-V side of the fusion (Figure 2A), suggesting that rex sites are unique elements of the X-chromosome that are required for TAD formation.
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 2A Hi-C data.

claim: Rex sites are unique elements of the X-chromosome that are required for TAD formation.
source: First, there are no noticeable TADs on chromosome-V side of the fusion (Figure 2A), suggesting that rex sites are unique elements of the X-chromosome that are required for TAD formation.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that no TADs form on chromosome-V despite condensin DC spreading.

claim: Enrichment of DNA contacts closer to the main diagonal occur specifically for the chromosome-V side of the X;V fusion.
source: Second, enrichment of DNA contacts closer to the main diagonal occur specifically for the chromosome-V side of the fusion (Figure 2A, third panel), which coincides with the decrease in mean loop size (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 2A and 2B.

claim: There is weakening of checker-board pattern on chromosome-V side of the X;V fusion.
source: Third, weakening of checker-board pattern on chromosome-V side (Figure 2A, inset), which coincides with the local decrease in sub-compartment strength (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 2A inset and Figure 2C.

claim: The spreading of condensin DC is partially a reflection of loop extrusion.
source: In summary, the spreading of condensin DC is partially a reflection of loop extrusion, which cannot sufficiently create TADs without the presence of rex sites.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the X;V fusion Hi-C data.

claim: Rex sites are bidirectional barriers to loop extrusion.
source: Therefore, unlike CTCF binding sites, rex sites are bidirectional barriers to loop extrusion.
evidence: This is concluded from the rex-8 orientation insertion experiment shown in Figure 3.

claim: The rex-rex corner-peaks and the new boundary on either side of the inserted rex-8 were similar regardless of the orientation of insertion.
source: The rex-rex corner-peaks and the new boundary on either side of the inserted rex-8 were similar regardless of the orientation of insertion (Figure 3).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 3 Hi-C data.

claim: Insertion of a single rex-8 on chromosome-II resulted in recruitment but not spreading of condensin DC.
source: The insertion of a single strong rex-8 on chromosome-II resulted in recruitment but not spreading of condensin DC.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by ChIP-seq data in Figure 5A.

claim: Insertion of combination of rex-1 and rex-8 leads to both recruitment and spreading.
source: Insertion of combination of rex-1 and rex-8 leads to both recruitment and spreading (Figure 5A, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A), suggesting the of rex sites also behave cooperatively in regards to spreading from the rex sites.
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A ChIP-seq data.

claim: Rex sites behave cooperatively in regards to spreading from the rex sites.
source: Insertion of combination of rex-1 and rex-8 leads to both recruitment and spreading (Figure 5A, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A), suggesting the of rex sites also behave cooperatively in regards to spreading from the rex sites.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that multiple rex sites lead to more spreading than single rex sites.

claim: Insertion of the super rex was sufficient to recruit condensin DC as a point source and led to spreading of condensin DC more than that of the single rex-8.
source: Insertion of the super rex indeed was sufficient to recruit condensin DC as a point source and led to spreading of condensin DC more than that of the single rex-8 (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 5A ChIP-seq data.

claim: Rex sites are loading sites for condensin DC in addition to being bidirectional barriers.
source: Therefore, we conclude that rex sites are loading sites for condensin DC in addition to being bidirectional barriers.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the ectopic insertion experiments showing recruitment and cooperative behavior.

claim: Condensin DC represses transcription initiation by a factor of ~2 across the entire X-chromosomes.
source: Condensin DC represses transcription initiation by a factor of ~2 across the entire X-chromosomes (Kruesi et al., 2013; Kramer et al., 2016; Kramer et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the results with citations to previous work.

claim: The level of condensin DC binding is proportional to repression as seen in X;A fusion chromosomes.
source: The level of condensin DC binding is proportional to repression as seen in X;A fusion chromosomes (Street et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the results with citation to previous work.

claim: Genes were not individually repressed by condensin DC in ectopic recruitment experiments, but there was a measurable effect when changes were analyzed at the domain level within ~200 and ~500 kb bins and even at the chromosomal level.
source: We performed mRNA-seq in two rex insertion strains and observed that genes were not individually repressed by condensin DC, but there was a measurable effect when changes were analyzed at the domain level within ~200 and ~500 kb bins and even at the chromosomal level (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: Condensin DC induces domain-wide repression whose effect size is proportional to the level of condensin DC binding.
source: This supports the idea that condensin DC induces domain-wide repression whose effect size is proportional to the level of condensin DC binding.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the mRNA-seq data in ectopic insertion strains.

claim: Insertion of a single rex-8 created a TAD boundary on the X but not on chromosome II.
source: Insertion of a single rex-8 created a TAD boundary on the X (Figure 3) but not on chromosome II (Figure 6).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figures 3 and 6 Hi-C data.

claim: Inserted rex-8 did not serve as an indiscriminate loop extrusion barrier for other SMC complexes.
source: Therefore, inserted rex-8 did not serve as an indiscriminate loop extrusion barrier for other SMC complexes.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that single rex-8 on chromosome II does not form TAD boundary.

claim: Insertion of strong rex sites (rex-47, rex-8, or rex-14) on chromosome-I does not result in boundary formation.
source: This is in agreement with previous work showing that insertion of strong rex sites (rex-47, rex-8, or rex-14) on chromosome-I does not result in boundary formation (Anderson et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the results with citation to previous work.

claim: Flames emanate from super rex insertion site.
source: Consistent with one-sided extrusion, we observe flames emanating from super rex (Figure 6).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 6 Hi-C data.

claim: Flames off the endogenous strong rex sites are apparent on the X-chromosome.
source: The flames off the endogenous strong rex sites are also apparent on the X-chromosome (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 1C.

claim: An insulation effect is observed at the super rex.
source: Additionally, we observe an insulation effect at the super rex.
evidence: This is stated in the results and can be inferred from Figure 6 Hi-C data.

claim: In the three-rex insertion, all features of TADs are observed, including enriched square contacts, insulation, flame, and corner peak.
source: Third, the three rex insertion, where there are both recruitment and spreading from multiple sources. In the three-rex insertion, we observe all features of TADs, including enriched square contacts, insulation, flame, and corner peak (Figure 6).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 6 Hi-C data.

claim: A flame that extends past the right rex-8 implies that a subset of one-sided LEFs loaded on the left rex-8 can move past the right rex-8, suggesting a probabilistic barrier function by the rex sites.
source: A flame that extends past the right rex-8 implies that a subset of one-sided LEFs loaded on the left rex-8 can move past the right rex-8, suggesting a probabilistic barrier function by the rex sites.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the Hi-C data in Figure 6.

claim: The spreading of condensin DC observed in super rex and three rex insertions coincides with the local increase in the insulation score compared to the wildtype.
source: When zoomed out, the spreading of condensin DC observed in super rex and three rex insertions coincides with the local increase in the insulation score compared to the wildtype (Figure 6—figure supplement 1, red arrows).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Observed changes in 3D structure are not simply a redistribution of existing contact frequencies but rather a formation of additional contacts.
source: This suggests that observed changes in 3D structure are not simply a redistribution of existing contact frequencies but rather a formation of additional contacts.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the insulation score analysis.

claim: The facilitation of 3D contacts that coincides with the spreading of condensin DC along with the relative insulation at the ectopic rex sites supports a model based on loop extrusion by condensin DC.
source: In summary, the facilitation of 3D contacts that coincides with the spreading of condensin DC along with the relative insulation at the ectopic rex sites supports a model based on loop extrusion by condensin DC.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the Hi-C and ChIP-seq data in ectopic insertion experiments.

claim: Cooperativity between rex sites ensures X-specific and robust binding of condensin DC to an entire chromosome.
source: In previous work, we proposed that cooperation between rex sites ensures X-specific and robust binding of condensin DC to an entire chromosome (Albritton and Ercan, 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citation to previous work.

claim: The cooperativity of rex sites is also involved in spreading.
source: Our ChIP-seq analysis of spreading in ectopic insertion strains suggests that the cooperativity is also involved in spreading.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion based on the ChIP-seq data from ectopic insertions.

claim: Cooperativity of rex sites must be distance dependent.
source: Therefore, cooperativity must be distance dependent.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from comparing results of three rex insertions at different distances.

claim: A previous attempt of three rex insertions spaced far apart (within 3 MB) resulted in weak recruitment of DCC and no changes on Hi-C matrix.
source: A previous attempt of three rex insertions spaced far apart (within 3 MB) resulted in weak recruitment of DCC and no changes on Hi-C matrix (Anderson et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citation to previous work.

claim: Even with a super rex insertion that recruited at a level comparable rex sites on the X, the level of spreading remained lower than that of the endogenous X-chromosome.
source: Indeed, even with a super rex insertion that recruited at a level comparable rex sites on the X, the level of spreading remained lower than that of the endogenous X-chromosome.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and can be inferred from ChIP-seq data in Figure 5A.

claim: On the X, activity of many weaker rex sites in between the 1 MB distance (average between strong rex sites) may contribute to the robust recruitment and spreading of condensin DC.
source: On the X, activity of many weaker rex sites in between the 1 MB distance (average between strong rex sites) may contribute to the robust recruitment and spreading of condensin DC.
evidence: This is a speculation stated in the discussion.

claim: Many segments of the X-chromosomes cannot autonomously recruit condensin DC.
source: Unlike rex sites, many other segments of the X-chromosomes cannot autonomously recruit condensin DC (Jans et al., 2009; Csankovszki et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citations to previous work.

claim: Condensin DC must 'spread' from rex to other sites on the X-chromosomes.
source: Thus, condensin DC must 'spread' from rex to other sites on the X-chromosomes.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that many X segments cannot autonomously recruit condensin DC.

claim: Spreading phenomenon was observed on X;A fusion chromosomes.
source: Such 'spreading' phenomenon was later observed on X;A fusion chromosomes (Ercan et al., 2009; Pferdehirt et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citations to previous work.

claim: If rex sites were preferential loading sites for a two-sided LEF, one would observe a secondary perpendicular diagonal which is not present in the Hi-C data.
source: If rex sites were preferential loading sites for a two-sided LEF, one would observe a secondary perpendicular diagonal which is not present in the Hi-C data.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as reasoning for the model.

claim: Condensin DC is proposed to be a one-sided LEF based on the presence of flames and the absence of a perpendicular diagonal.
source: We begin by proposing that condensin DC is a one-sided LEF based on the presence of flames and the absence of a perpendicular diagonal.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as part of the proposed model.

claim: In simulation, one-sided LEFs cannot form corner-peaks due to high frequency of gaps between two oppositely oriented LEFs.
source: In simulation, one-sided LEFs cannot form corner-peaks due to high frequency of gaps between two oppositely oriented LEFs (Banigan et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citation to previous work.

claim: In simulation, the corner-peaks can be 'rescued' with strong preferential loading at the boundary.
source: This is unlikely to be a limitation in our system, because (i) in simulation, the corner-peaks can be 'rescued' with strong preferential loading at the boundary and (ii) a recent preprint reported that the cleavage of DPY-26, a kleisin subunit shared by condensin I and DC, did not eliminate rex-rex corner-peaks (Das, 2022).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citation.

claim: The cleavage of DPY-26, a kleisin subunit shared by condensin I and DC, did not eliminate rex-rex corner-peaks.
source: This is unlikely to be a limitation in our system, because (i) in simulation, the corner-peaks can be 'rescued' with strong preferential loading at the boundary and (ii) a recent preprint reported that the cleavage of DPY-26, a kleisin subunit shared by condensin I and DC, did not eliminate rex-rex corner-peaks (Das, 2022).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citation to a preprint.

claim: The loss of SDC-2 does not result in global redistribution of condensin DC.
source: However, the loss of SDC-2 does not result in global redistribution of condensin DC; in the absence of SDC-2, the fluorescence recovery after photobleaching (FRAP) recovery of condensin DC shows similar dynamics to that of free-floating molecules (Breimann et al., 2022).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citation to previous work.

claim: It has been proposed that the condensin DC loaders also 'spread,' although to a lesser extent than condensin DC, leading to SDC-2, SDC-3, and DPY-30 enrichment at active promoters on the X-chromosome.
source: It has been proposed that the condensin DC loaders also 'spread,' although to a lesser extent than condensin DC, leading to SDC-2, SDC-3, and DPY-30 enrichment at active promoters on the X-chromosome (Ercan et al., 2007; Albritton et al., 2017; Street et al., 2019; Pferdehirt et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citations to previous work.

claim: The number of SDC-2 binding sites on X-chromosome is an order of magnitude below that of condensin DC subunits.
source: However, as can be seen from Figure 1B and previous peak analysis (Albritton et al., 2017), the number of SDC-2 (the hermaphrodite specific protein that initiates condensin DC recruitment to the X) binding sites on X-chromosome is an order of magnitude below that of condensin DC subunits.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with reference to Figure 1B and citation.

claim: Upon loading, condensin DC may begin one-sided loop extrusion, but the inactive loop-anchor at the rex site is prone to being displaced.
source: We propose that upon loading, condensin DC may begin one-sided loop extrusion, but the inactive loop-anchor at the rex site is prone to being displaced.
evidence: This is part of the proposed model stated in the discussion.

claim: One-sided loop extrusion from a loading site whose inactive anchor is prone to displacement by diffusion results in an increasingly murkier flame with increasing rate of diffusion.
source: This model is inspired from the simulation work by Banigan et al., 2020, which informs that one-sided loop extrusion from a loading site whose inactive anchor is prone to displacement by diffusion (semi-diffusive one-sided loop extrusion (LE) model with a loading site) results in an increasingly murkier flame with increasing rate of diffusion (Banigan et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citation to simulation work.

claim: Movement of the inactive anchor would allow condensin DC to form transient loops between two non-rex elements forming increased contacts within TADs.
source: Movement of the inactive anchor would allow condensin DC to form transient loops between two non-rex elements forming increased contacts within TADs.
evidence: This is part of the proposed model stated in the discussion.

claim: PQN-85 (NIPBL homolog in C. elegans) is enriched at the rex sites.
source: A candidate SMC complex displacing condensin DC loop anchor is cohesin, whose loader/processivity factor PQN-85 (NIPBL homolog in C. elegans) is enriched at the rex sites (Kranz et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citation to previous work.

claim: DCC localizes to and represses X-chromosome in the early stages of embryo development (~40 cells).
source: Previous work showed that DCC localizes to and represses X-chromosome in the early stages of embryo development (~40 cells) (Kramer et al., 2015; Dawes et al., 1999).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citations to previous work.

claim: Upon degradation of SDC-3 or cleavage of kleisin subunit DPY-26, TADs disappear but the rex-rex corner peaks remain unperturbed.
source: Hi-C data in a recent preprint presented that upon degradation of SDC-3 or cleavage of kleisin subunit DPY-26, TADs disappear but the rex-rex corner peaks remain unperturbed (Das, 2022).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citation to a preprint.

claim: Genetic loss of SDC-2 results in the complete loss of all features of TADs.
source: This is in contrast to the genetic loss of SDC-2 resulting in the complete loss of all features of TADs (Crane et al., 2015; Anderson et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citations to previous work.

claim: Genes located at the autosomal spreading region in the X;V fusion chromosome are repressed due to condensin DC spreading.
source: Previously, we showed that genes located at the autosomal spreading region in the X;V fusion chromosome are repressed due to condensin DC spreading (Street et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citation to previous work.

claim: Repression in X;V fusion does not coincide with TAD formation on the chromosome-V side.
source: Here, we show that this repression does not coincide with TAD formation on the chromosome-V side, and despite a clear loop-anchored TAD in three rex insertions, there was minimal effect on transcription.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion based on Hi-C and mRNA-seq data.

claim: Despite a clear loop-anchored TAD in three rex insertions, there was minimal effect on transcription.
source: Here, we show that this repression does not coincide with TAD formation on the chromosome-V side, and despite a clear loop-anchored TAD in three rex insertions, there was minimal effect on transcription.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion based on mRNA-seq data in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: Deletion of the eight strong rex sites did not result in changes in Hi-C distance decay curve.
source: Consistent with this idea, deletion of the eight strong rex sites did not result in changes in Hi-C distance decay curve, implying that the loop extrusion activity of condensin DC is largely unperturbed (Anderson et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citation to previous work.

claim: Shortening of 3D contacts indicative of condensin DC loop extrusion in the X;V fusion chromosome coincides with repression.
source: Similarly, shortening of 3D contacts indicative of condensin DC loop extrusion in the X;V fusion chromosome coincides with repression.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion based on Hi-C and previous expression data.

claim: Upon TOP-2 depletion, the processivity of condensin DC loop extrusion reduces, and the spreading of the complex to the chromosome also reduces.
source: Consistent with this idea, upon TOP-2 depletion, the processivity of condensin DC loop extrusion reduces, and the spreading of the complex to the chromosome also reduces (Morao et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citation to previous work.

claim: A null mutant of dpy-21 (a non condensin DCC subunit) results in X upregulation without significantly altering Hi-C interactions.
source: In agreement with this, a null mutant of dpy-21 (a non condensin DCC subunit) results in X upregulation without significantly altering Hi-C interactions (Breimann et al., 2022).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citation to previous work.

claim: C. elegans autosomes lack clear TAD boundaries.
source: However, since yeast chromosomes support much smaller interaction domains and lack clear TAD boundaries, how condensin binding regulates larger eukaryotic genomes remains unknown.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by Hi-C data in Figure 1B.

claim: C. elegans lacks a CTCF homolog.
source: In C. elegans, while cohesin is present, a CTCF homolog is absent (Heger et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the results with citation to previous work.

claim: No strong TAD structures are present on autosomes in C. elegans.
source: Therefore, no strong TAD structures are present on autosomes (Figure 1B, chromosome-I) as previously reported (Crane et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the results with reference to Figure 1B and citation.

claim: Condensin DC spreads ~3 MB into the autosomal region of X;V fusion chromosome.
source: Condensin DC spreads ~3 MB into the autosomal region of X;V fusion chromosome.
evidence: This is stated in Figure 2A caption and shown in ChIP-seq data.

claim: The level of condensin DC binding in the autosomes is lower than that of the X in ectopic recruitment experiments.
source: In ectopic recruitment experiments, the level of condensin DC binding in the autosomes is lower than that of the X (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 5A ChIP-seq data.

claim: Increasing the number of ectopic rex sites increases the mean DPY-27 ChIP signal and the number of peaks on chromosome-II in both L3 and embryos.
source: Contrary to this prediction, increasing the number of ectopic rex sites increases the mean DPY-27 ChIP signal and the number of peaks on chromosome-II in both L3 (Figure 5B) and embryos (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The presence of two flanking bidirectional barriers, rex-8, enhances binding at rex-1.
source: Again, contrary to this prediction, we observe that the presence of two flanking bidirectional barriers, rex-8, enhances binding at rex-1 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C) and minimally affects binding at rex-8 (Figure 5C, Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: ChIP-seq binding levels tightly follow the results of quantitative ChIP experiments performed in the three rex insertion embryos.
source: Importantly, ChIP-seq binding levels here tightly follow the results of quantitative ChIP experiments performed in the three rex insertion embryos (Albritton et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the results with citation to previous work.

claim: Rex sites behave more cooperatively than competitively as observed by recruitment at the rex sites.
source: Therefore, rex sites behave more cooperatively than competitively as observed by recruitment at the rex sites.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the ChIP-seq data in ectopic insertion experiments.

claim: Insertion of a weaker rex (rex-1) results in no recruitment or spreading.
